html:
The Belgian Revolution began in Brussels on 25 August 1830, when an opera about a revolt in Naples set off riots. The southern provinces broke away from the Netherlands and became the Kingdom of Belgium.

After Napoleon, the Congress of Vienna had joined the Catholic south to the Protestant north in the United Kingdom of the Netherlands under King William I. Catholics, French speakers and liberals resented his rule. Dutch troops failed to retake Brussels in September 1830.

The great powers recognised Belgian independence, and a German prince became King Leopold I in 1831. Belgium had one of the most liberal constitutions of its day. The Dutch accepted the split only in the Treaty of London of 1839, which guaranteed Belgian neutrality. See Belgium.
